claims.text: Surface compositional segregation triggers formation of a molten surface layer in solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
The molten surface layer initiates and governs the overall premelting-to-melting phase transition.
As-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have inherent surface compositional variations.
A passivating capping layer can suppress surface segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
In situ high-temperature TEM can be used to observe nanoparticle evolution during heating.
The comparison will be conducted under inert atmosphere while systematically varying heating ramp rate through the premelting and melting regimes.
The structural mediator is a progressively developing surface-molten layer caused by compositional segregation.
At elevated temperatures, selected elemental species preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Preferential surface segregation lowers the local melting-onset temperature.
Localized surface melting propagates inward and provides the pathway for the particle's overall phase transition.
Unmodified nanoparticles will develop a molten surface layer earlier than passivated nanoparticles.
Unmodified nanoparticles will have a lower DSC melting-onset temperature than passivated nanoparticles.
Suppressing segregation with passivation will delay surface melting.
The proposed behavior is expected under inert atmosphere and controlled heating rates in the premelting-to-melting regime.
Other phase-change mechanisms or thermal effects introduced by the passivating layer may cause deviations from the prediction.
The quantitative melting-onset shift and progression dynamics are uncertain.
Multielement interactions and limited imaging or calorimetric resolution may complicate characterization of the transition.
Similar DSC onset temperatures in passivated and unmodified particles, together with no discernible molten surface layer in TEM, would falsify the proposed segregation-governed transition.
